title: Reliably reverse advanced atherosclerosis throughout the arterial tree

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a treatment capability that makes advanced atherosclerosis extensively and durably reversible across the body’s arteries. It would resolve established plaques while restoring stable, functional arterial structure, including in arteries with advanced fibrotic and calcified disease. Safe repair would require preserving vessel integrity, avoiding plaque rupture and thrombosis, and controlling recurrence. These are proposed requirements for the breakthrough. The supplied evidence establishes a narrower foundation in coronary plaque treatment.

Existing lipid-lowering treatment provides a starting point. The FITTER report describes reductions in recurrent coronary events with statin treatment and summarizes evidence that lipid lowering can produce plaque regression and improve plaque composition over time. The proposed advance extends that foundation to extensive repair of advanced disease, with durable structural and functional benefits across multiple vascular territories.

significance.text: Conditional on successful development, extensive plaque resolution and stable arterial repair would make a widespread, cumulative disease substantially reversible. The direct achievement would be recovery of diseased arterial structure and function. The coronary rationale for pursuing this is substantial. FITTER explains that, after treatment of the culprit lesion in acute coronary syndrome, many recurrent myocardial infarctions arise from other pre-existing atherosclerotic lesions. Treating this residual disease could therefore have consequences beyond the initially treated site.

Conditional impact synthesis. Fewer myocardial infarctions, ischemic strokes and cardiovascular deaths are plausible downstream goals if repair safely reduces clinically important disease in the relevant arteries. Each benefit would require clinical demonstration. Plaque reversal would leave other causes of these events to be addressed, and an improvement in plaque imaging alone would leave the magnitude of clinical benefit unresolved. The supplied coronary trial provides no demonstrated whole-body repair, stroke-prevention or mortality benefit.

The extent of the achievement would depend on which lesions, patients and arterial territories respond, how much function is recovered, and how long the repair lasts. Several successfully treated territories could demonstrate broad applicability. A finite set of observations would still leave questions about efficacy in additional arterial beds and lesion types.

missing_breakthrough.text: Proposed capability gap. The central challenge is to achieve extensive, durable regression together with stable repair in people who already have advanced atherosclerosis. The engineering target includes fibrotic and calcified lesions, preservation of vessel integrity during treatment, avoidance of rupture, thrombosis and vessel injury, and sustained control of recurrence. The supplied evidence does not establish the technical feasibility of resolving each of these lesion components or the comprehensive availability of such treatment.

Scientific and engineering synthesis. A convincing intervention would need to coordinate removal or remodeling of diseased material with maintenance of a mechanically stable arterial wall. It would also need to produce beneficial structural change alongside preserved or improved physiological function. Addressing one plaque feature leaves the response of other components unresolved, so lipid depletion, fibrosis, calcification and vessel function would need separate assessment where relevant.

Proposed translational barriers include achieving consistent effects across different vascular territories and advanced lesion types, identifying patients who benefit, establishing a practical treatment regimen, and sustaining repair under continuing disease risk. FITTER contributes evidence about short-term coronary treatment and explicitly calls for longer follow-up and clinical-outcome assessment. Its scope leaves advanced fibrotic and calcified disease, whole-tree repair and long-term recurrence control incompletely documented.

current_state.text: Partial plaque regression is already possible. The FITTER authors summarize prior GLAGOV, PACMAN-AMI and HUYGENS findings as showing incremental plaque regression when PCSK9 inhibitors were added to high-intensity statin therapy. They also describe statin-associated reductions in recurrent events and improvements in plaque composition over time. These earlier trial findings are available here through FITTER’s account. Their underlying publications were outside the supplied review’s inspected materials.

The randomized, placebo-controlled FITTER trial, published on 18 August 2025, assigned 150 patients with acute coronary syndrome and relevant non-culprit coronary lesions to evolocumab or placebo added to high-intensity statin therapy. Over 12 weeks, neither primary endpoint showed a statistically significant between-group improvement. The reported p-values were 0.6 for fractional flow reserve and 0.8 for maximum lipid core burden index within a 4 mm segment.

Fractional flow reserve is a pressure-based measure of coronary lesion physiology. The maximum lipid core burden index within a 4 mm segment characterizes a localized plaque lipid feature. Together, these endpoints assess selected physiological and morphological aspects of coronary disease. They leave extensive structural repair across the arterial tree untested. The 12-week findings also leave longer treatment durations and other interventions open to investigation. FITTER’s authors explicitly call for longer follow-up and assessment of clinical outcomes.

The supplied review assessed the full, untruncated main article text, including methods and tabulated results. Linked supplements and figure images were outside its inspected materials. The text and tables supported the reported trial population, duration and primary comparisons. The supplied record contains no bounded freshness-search results, so it cannot establish the comprehensive treatment landscape or whether the full proposed capability remained unavailable as of 1 November 2026. Its source retrieval date of 11 November 2026 adds no evidence about intervening developments.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. Show extensive regression and stable arterial repair in people with advanced atherosclerosis across several prespecified vascular territories, with deliberate inclusion and characterization of fibrotic and calcified disease. Before testing, define the required magnitude of regression, the structural and functional measures of repair, the follow-up duration needed to demonstrate durability, and acceptable safety thresholds. These are proposed assessment requirements whose numerical values remain to be established.
completion_criteria.label: Extensive regression and stable arterial repair across prespecified vascular territories

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical confirmation. Randomized trials against excellent contemporary care should demonstrate fewer clinically important cardiovascular events with acceptable safety. Prespecified analyses should establish which outcomes improve and in which populations, including myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke or mortality where those benefits are claimed. Longer follow-up should assess persistence of repair, recurrent plaque disease and delayed harms. FITTER supports the need for longer follow-up and clinical-outcome assessment, while the broader completion framework is a proposal.
completion_criteria.label: Randomized trials demonstrate fewer cardiovascular events with acceptable safety

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries. Independent teams should reproduce the principal structural, functional and clinical findings using transparent measurement methods. Studies should document the treatment burden, eligibility limits, maintenance requirements and performance across the tested lesion types and vascular territories. Any claim of broad applicability should state its demonstrated coverage and remaining gaps. Finite testing would establish demonstrated breadth, with further evidence needed for additional arterial beds and patient groups.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproduction of principal findings with documented practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. CAR-12, Detect actionable coronary plaque risk before a first clinical event, overlaps most directly through identification of plaques and patients who could benefit from intervention. Its central capability is early risk detection and actionability. CAR-02 concerns reversal and repair of established advanced disease. Detection could support treatment selection and monitoring, while each concept retains its own completion requirements.

Roster-based synthesis. CAR-10, Reverse established calcific aortic stenosis without valve replacement, shares the ambition of reversing established cardiovascular pathology and may involve related questions about calcified tissue remodeling. CAR-10 targets aortic valve disease, while CAR-02 targets atherosclerotic disease in arterial walls. CAR-11, Reverse pulmonary arterial hypertension and its cardiovascular consequences, shares an interest in vascular repair and physiological recovery, with a distinct pulmonary vascular disease target.

Roster-based synthesis. CAR-01, Regenerate a severely damaged adult human heart, and CAR-08, Durably reverse heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, concern myocardial recovery and heart-failure physiology. Arterial repair could complement those goals where atherosclerotic disease contributes to cardiac injury or dysfunction. Each would still require direct evidence for recovery of its target condition.

Roster-based synthesis. CAR-03, A durable, broadly affordable total artificial heart, CAR-04, A dependable supply of transplantable animal hearts, and CAR-07, Produce a transplantable, fully engineered living human heart, address replacement of severely diseased hearts. Their overlap with CAR-02 lies in reducing the consequences of cardiovascular disease. Their completion depends on replacement-heart performance, availability and durability, whereas CAR-02 requires repair of the patient’s arterial disease. Systemic arterial health could remain relevant after heart replacement.

Roster-based synthesis. CAR-05, Correct inherited heart disease directly and durably in the beating heart, shares the goal of durable disease modification, with an inherited cardiac target. CAR-06, Make most preventable sudden cardiac deaths predictable and preventable, and CAR-09, A durable, non-ablative cure for atrial fibrillation, address prediction and prevention of sudden death and treatment of an arrhythmia, respectively. Successful arterial repair could affect some ischemia-related risks, while those concepts encompass additional mechanisms and require their own demonstrations.

Roster-based synthesis. CAR-13, Broadly prevent cardiac injury from cancer treatment without weakening cancer control, overlaps through cardiovascular injury prevention and preservation of cardiac health. Its defining requirement includes protection during cancer treatment while maintaining cancer control. CAR-02 instead targets established advanced atherosclerotic disease across the arterial tree.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence cannot establish whether extensive, durable repair of advanced atherosclerosis across the arterial tree remained unavailable as of 1 November 2026.
The technical basis and feasibility of safely resolving advanced fibrotic and calcified arterial lesions require evidence beyond the supplied coronary trial.
Numerical thresholds for extensive regression, stable repair, durability and acceptable safety remain unspecified.
The vascular territories, lesion types and patient populations needed to substantiate broad applicability remain to be defined.
The magnitude of any benefit for myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, mortality and long-term recurrence remains undemonstrated for the proposed capability.
Linked FITTER supplements, figure images and the original publications of the prior regression trials were outside the supplied review’s inspected materials.

brief.title: Lasting repair of diseased arteries throughout the body
possible: People with advanced artery disease could have plaques, the deposits that build up in artery walls, extensively cleared or reshaped throughout the body. Treatment would restore stable, working arteries, including those with scar-like tissue and hardened calcium deposits.
The repair would last, with treatment controlling the return of plaques while preserving artery walls and avoiding plaque rupture and blood clots.
why: For people with advanced disease, this would mean recovering artery structure and function after years of accumulating damage.

Repair across the body could reduce heart attacks, strokes caused by blocked blood flow, and cardiovascular deaths. Treating disease beyond an initially treated blockage matters because many repeat heart attacks arise from other existing plaques.

sources.showed: The FITTER trial tested evolocumab, a cholesterol-lowering drug, added to intensive statin treatment. After 12 weeks, it found no statistically significant added improvement in pressure-based blood-flow measurements or plaque fat content in heart arteries.
sources.quote: No between-group differences in any IVUS-derived parameter were found.
sources.cited_for: Partial plaque regression is possible, but this short trial found no added improvement on its main measures.
sources.not_established: The trial did not establish lasting repair of advanced plaques throughout the body or fewer cardiovascular events from such repair.

sources.showed: In a selected group of 33 people, cholesterol-lowering treatment reduced plaque fat in the carotid arteries in the neck. Imaging also showed a reduction in the proportion of the artery occupied by its wall in fat-rich regions.
sources.quote: Intensive lipid therapy significantly depletes carotid plaque lipid.
sources.cited_for: Cholesterol-lowering treatment can reduce plaque fat and produce partial regression in neck arteries.
sources.not_established: This small analysis did not establish extensive repair of advanced scarred or calcified plaques across the body's arteries.

shown: Partial plaque shrinkage is already possible with cholesterol-lowering treatment. Xue-Qiao Zhao and colleagues used magnetic resonance imaging, which produces detailed internal images, to track reduced plaque fat and partial regression in neck arteries in a selected group of 33 people.

Frans B Mensink and colleagues tested additional cholesterol lowering in people with significant heart-artery disease. FITTER found no statistically significant added benefit on its main blood-flow and plaque-fat measures over 12 weeks.
missing: No treatment has demonstrated extensive, lasting repair of advanced plaques across several artery regions, including scarred and calcified disease.
Repair must preserve artery strength and function without causing plaque rupture, blood clots or vessel injury.
Trials must establish whether this repair reduces major cardiovascular events and keeps disease from returning over the long term.

milestones.label: Extensive, stable repair across several artery regions
milestones.explanation: Studies would have to show extensive, lasting plaque reduction and stable artery structure and function across predefined regions, including scarred and calcified disease. This would establish broad repair of advanced disease.

milestones.label: Fewer cardiovascular events with acceptable safety
milestones.explanation: Randomized trials would have to show fewer major cardiovascular events than excellent current care, with acceptable safety and lasting benefits. This would establish that repair improves health beyond changes on scans.

milestones.label: Independent confirmation and clear treatment limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce structural, functional and clinical benefits using transparent measures and document eligibility, treatment burden, maintenance and coverage. This would establish reliability and practical limits.

uncertain: It remains unclear whether advanced scarred and calcified plaques can be safely resolved while maintaining a strong, functional artery wall.
The required amount of plaque reduction, duration of repair and acceptable safety thresholds remain undefined.
Which artery regions, plaque types and patient groups would establish broad applicability remains unresolved.
